title: Java I/O Streams Overview
learningObjectives: Distinguish byte streams from character-based readers and writers
Identify the source and destination of each I/O operation
Explain when text decoding and encoding take place
Describe how buffering reduces repeated low-level I/O operations
Close application-owned I/O resources using structured cleanup

understand.concept: Byte streams process raw bytes and suit binary content; character streams decode or encode text. Buffered wrappers reduce low-level operations. Close owned resources with try-with-resources.
understand.whyItMatters: Java I/O Streams Overview helps learners create Java applications that are easier to reason about, test and maintain.
understand.analogy: Treat the concept as a clearly labeled tool for one programming responsibility.
understand.analogyLimit: Actual behavior is defined by Java language rules and API contracts.

explain.narrative:
## Java I/O Streams Overview

Byte streams process raw bytes and suit binary content; character streams decode or encode text. Buffered wrappers reduce low-level operations. Close owned resources with try-with-resources.

Identify the input and desired result. Select the Java construct or API that supports the requirement. Keep code readable, handle documented failures and state assumptions clearly.

Compile with JDK 21, predict output before running, and test normal, boundary and invalid inputs.

examples.title: Core API
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { byte[] bytes = {65, 66, 67}; System.out.println(bytes.length); } }
examples.explanation: A byte stream handles raw bytes.

examples.title: Practical use
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { String text = "ABC"; try (var reader = new java.io.StringReader(text)) { System.out.println((char) reader.read()); } } }
examples.explanation: A character reader returns decoded characters.

examples.title: Boundary behavior
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var in = new java.io.ByteArrayInputStream(new byte[]{1,2,3})) { System.out.println(in.read()); } } }
examples.explanation: Shows input flowing from a source into the program.

examples.title: Alternative pattern
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (var out = new java.io.ByteArrayOutputStream()) { out.write(65); System.out.println(out.toByteArray()[0]); } } }
examples.explanation: Shows output flowing from the program to a destination.

examples.title: Verify the result
examples.code: public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.println("BufferedReader".startsWith("Buffered")); } }
examples.explanation: Introduces a buffered wrapper by name; later examples demonstrate its behavior.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small program that copies bytes from ByteArrayInputStream to ByteArrayOutputStream and text from StringReader to StringWriter. Compare the APIs.
practise.independentTask: Create a diagram of source → input stream/reader → program → output stream/writer → destination. Label where byte decoding and encoding occur.
hints: Choose the API that matches the data representation and operation.
Test empty, normal and failure cases; verify exact output or file contents.
practise.challenge: Choose byte or character streams for an image, a UTF-8 text file and a serialized binary record. Justify each choice and resource ownership.
